item.title: How to Lie with Statistics
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

How to Lie with Statistics

Five ways that statistics can be unfairly presented.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • If you have heard that it is possible to lie with statistics, you would be correct.
  • There are several ways that researchers might misrepresent their data with statistics.
  • Here are five specific ways that researchers might "lie" with statistics. Keep an eye out for them!
Source: Chazottes / Pexels

Any psychology curriculum includes considerable training in statistics. I first taught statistics in 1996, and I have enjoyed teaching it ever since. Students are often surprised at how versatile and applicable this content is. Understanding statistics can help us better understand practical issues such as housing market trends, weather conditions, bird behavior at the feeder, the timing of blossoms in one's garden, people's behavior, our own behavior and internal workings, and more. Ultimately, statistics is a tool to understand the world around us. When students ask, "Why do I have to take statistics?" I am prepared with answers.

People often hear about "lying with statistics." While this topic is an issue, statistical inferences should be taken seriously. When examining information based on statistical processes, we need to ask certain questions to help us make sure the implications of the findings are warranted. Understanding statistics at a basic level helps ensure we take in information based on statistical findings with our eyes wide open.

To help people keep an eye out for situations in which someone might be "lying with statistics," here are five specific issues to watch out for when presented with statistical findings of any kind:

  1. The Amplification of Small Effect Sizes

    Most statistical processes yield both "effect sizes" and information on "statistical significance." In short, an effect size indicates how large the observed impact is; statistical significance speaks to whether it is likely that the effects obtained (however large they are) can be generalized to the broader population. As such, it is highly possible that a finding may be "statistically significant" even if it is a small effect size. For instance, a researcher might find that a drug designed to help people lose weight results in a statistically significant effect, with people taking the drug losing more weight than people taking a placebo. Yet the average difference in weight loss between the two groups might be only half a pound. Playing up the statistical significance, in this case, while neglecting to comment on the effect size, would be a bit dishonest.

  2. Insinuating Causation with Correlational Data

    Statistics, in and of itself, does not allow you to determine if one variable causes changes in another variable. The ability to infer causality is based on research design (such as the use of experimental methods) and not on statistical processes per se. That said, it is often the case that researchers who find statistical relationships among variables without using experimental methods may overstep in their verbiage. For instance, if a researcher found that household income is predictive of relatively high levels of exercise, it would be questionable if that researcher insinuated a causal relationship by saying something like "so having money seems to make people exercise more." As all psychology students (rightfully) hear from their professors, "correlation does not necessarily imply causation."

  3. Post-Hoc Alpha Level

    In many statistical processes, the researcher determines an "alpha level," which refers to the odds that an inference from a sample to a broader population might not be warranted. Researchers need to define that alpha level ahead of time and stick to that determination. If you obtain a finding that could be unreliable 3 percent of the time, and your alpha level was chosen as 1 percent from the outset, it would be problematic if you change your alpha level to 5 percent just to be able to say that your finding is "statistically reliable" and that the pattern that you found in a sample likely generalizes to the broader population.

  4. Post-Hoc Choosing of a One-Tailed Test

    In statistics, we often choose to use what is called a "one-tailed test" versus a "two-tailed test." In short, a one-tailed test should be used when you predict in a specific direction (for example, imagine a study that predicted drinking coffee before an exam corresponded to relatively high exam scores). A two-tailed test should be used when you are predicting a difference, but you do not specify the direction of that difference (for example, imagine designing the coffee-exam study to test whether coffee drinkers scored significantly higher or lower than everyone else). Given how our statistical processes operate, it is easier to obtain a statistically significant finding with a one-tailed test than with a two-tailed test. If you start with a two-tailed test, but obtain a result that is only significant if you use a one-tailed test, you are being dishonest with the data.

  5. A Statistical Fishing Expedition

    When we refer to a statistical fishing expedition, this is a study that includes a high number of statistical tests. By chance alone, some percentage of statistical tests will naturally show as statistically significant (implying that the findings in the sample represent how things are at the population level) even if the inference about the population is incorrect. If you conduct 100 statistical tests, by chance alone, some of the results will erroneously emerge as "statistically significant." These effects are considered spurious. If you conduct a high number of statistical tests, you, the researcher, need to take steps to reduce the possibility of presenting such spurious findings as meaningful.

Bottom Line

The statistics field provides extraordinary tools to help us understand the world around us. Including the psychological states and behaviors of ourselves and others. Can researchers lie with statistics? Unfortunately, yes! Getting educated in the basics of statistics can help us process statistical-based findings in a way that we can help us catch such "lies." Want to understand the world around us better? Take a course in statistics.

item.title: Falling Short In Life
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Falling Short In Life

Personal Perspective: Find the physical and emotional strength to get back up.

Posted November 18, 2026

In a family loss, peace can be found in a sunset on Cape Cod, knowing the sun will rise again…
Source: Photo by Greg O’Brien

We all fall short in life, and maybe that’s a good thing. Keeps us close to the Terra Firma.

Forgiveness of self and others, and the drive to press on in tough, wrenching times are coins of life. Pulitzer Prize-winning poet and journalist the late Carl Sandburg said years ago, “Time is the coin of life. It’s the only coin you have, and only you can determine how it will be spent.”

And that’s not pocket change. It’s a road map to success, though one that takes great persistence. I know firsthand from my life challenges. At 76 now, I’ve learned it’s not so much about the fall, but when and how you get back up—a humbling directive, though one that has helped me persevere through critical memory loss and advancing cancer, as others would know in their own trials.

I learned more about this recently in symbolic ways from my beautiful 40-year-old daughter Colleen, a writer and a teacher. November 16 was the 38th birthday of my late son Conor, who died several years ago from grand mal seizures and other issues. Conor traveled with me cross-country as a “guard dog,” as he called it, for speeches related to my book, On Pluto: Inside the Mind of Alzheimer’s. We were close, and in heavenly ways, closer now.

In a Facebook post on Conor’s birthday, shared also with son Brendan, Colleen—struggling through the emotion of this loss—wrote words that deeply touched my wife Mary Catherine and my soul—words that may touch you in losses in your lives.

Colleen wrote: “Happy Heavenly Birthday to my little brother, Conor, and my guardian angel. Your birthday is always especially hard for me because it makes me think of all the ‘could-haves’ and ‘should-be’s.’ But I feel you in the little things, the unexpected signs, and the moments that seem too coincidental to be anything else. I talk to you, I look for you, and I like to think you’re never far away.

“Losing someone changes the way you look at life and the people around you. It reminds you that everyone is carrying something we may never see. That life is incredibly fragile, that tomorrow is never promised, and that we don’t always get another opportunity to say what we wish we had said.

“I’ve learned how important it is to give people grace. To forgive, to let go of what weighs us down, to be kinder than we think we need to be, and to remember that none of us get through life without making mistakes. We don’t have to agree with everyone’s choices to show them compassion. We don’t have to understand someone’s struggles to remind them they’re not alone.

“Make the phone call. Send the text. Forgive when your heart is ready. Ask a second time if someone says they’re okay, but something tells you otherwise. Tell people you love them while you have the chance.

“I hope you’re proud of me, Conor. I hope you see how hard I’m trying. And I hope you know that no matter how much time passes, you will always be a part of me. Keep sending those signs. I’ll keep looking for them.

“Love you, always, Conor. Until we meet again, Colleen.”

As I reflect on Colleen’s comments and Conor’s birthday, I am reminded again that it is crucial to rise from the falls of life. And I’m trying.

item.title: When You Feel Like an Outsider at Your Own Holiday Gathering
item.description:
Family Dynamics

When You Feel Like an Outsider at Your Own Holiday Gathering

If you feel like an outsider among family and friends, you are not alone.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • A study of over 200,000 adults in 22 countries found that 14 percent felt like outsiders in their families.
  • Feelings of not belonging and disconnection may be even more pronounced during year-end.
  • We may feel like outsiders because our beliefs, lifestyle choices, or perspectives differ from others.

I remember feeling like an outsider as a kid. I didn't speak English and could not communicate with my classmates. I never wanted to go outside to play during recess or lunchtime. While others were excited to get out of the classroom, I just wanted to stay in because those walls were my refuge. The feeling of not belonging still surfaces in various contexts, especially when others share stories, backgrounds, and experiences, ones I cannot relate to. Being the single, childless Latina at family gatherings was tough. In a culture where marriage and kids have been the norm, it is easy for some of us to question our sense of belonging even when we are among family and friends.

Source: Askar Aba / Pexels

With the holiday season and social gatherings upon us, we may feel a mixture of joy and dread. Joy in gathering with those we love, but dread as we anticipate the questions and feelings of being an outsider that may surface. Some of us may feel like outsiders for distinct reasons, including not sharing the same marital status, parenting status, political beliefs, sexual orientation, religious beliefs, and perspectives. We may also feel like outsiders because people may relate to a version of ourselves that no longer exists. You feel like an impostor, trying to contort yourself into someone you are not. Consider the following steps.

  1. You are on a different journey.

“When are you going to get married and have kids?” This question was often on auto-play in the gatherings I attended. Regardless of harmless intent, it made me feel behind in life. Reaching a certain age and not having ticked the right boxes were a cause for concern; not for me, but for those around me. Once I realized that the expectations that other people had were a function of their own beliefs and experiences, which were not mine to adopt, I became less anxious about attending social functions. No journey is the same, and yours is no less valuable because it does not look like the path others have taken.

  1. Redirect the conversation.

Kids and marriage are two topics often discussed. People bring up certain topics because they may lack other news, not to make you feel left out. I realized this and offered other topics. If conversations make you uncomfortable, consider redirecting them. Ask about people’s upcoming travel plans, sports, hobbies, projects, celebrations, milestones, or share your own. Research finds that people like to talk about themselves. You can ask about their interests or a story or experience you have in common; this will ease anxiety about other topics. If they discuss something you are not familiar with, ask them to tell you about it.

  1. Feelings are not facts.

The narrative running in our heads may say we are outsiders, but it does not mean we are. Whether with friends or family, you have something in common. Reminisce about common themes and share updates about your life if you are comfortable. Every gathering is an opportunity to create new memories and share experiences. Perhaps next year, they will ask about something you shared this year or refer to the experience you are now having. But even if they do not, as President Obama once said, “Do not let people think you do not belong.” You have tremendous value by simply being you. Some contexts will see it, and others may not, but it is not your job to convince them.

Man sitting alone while group is gathered.
Source: Silver K Black / Pexels

If you feel like an outsider even when you are among family and friends, you are not alone. A study of over 200,000 adults across 22 countries found that 14 percent felt like outsiders in their families growing up and about 25 percent, one in four, in the U.S. Ironically, feelings of not belonging and disconnection may be even more pronounced during the holidays, which are marketed as a season of closeness, warmth, and togetherness. Just like filling the gas tank before a road trip, you can emotionally fill your tank before attending gatherings that have left you feeling uneasy in the past.

Draw on the support of the people who accept and know you as you show up, not an older or idealized version of yourself. If you arrive at a gathering and find yourself in conversations that make you question your sense of belonging, try to redirect the conversation toward a less sensitive topic. Assume good intentions. People don't normally mean to make you feel uncomfortable. They may be unaware that questions about your status—marital, biological, or any other type of clock—are not appropriate for discussion. If all else fails, excuse yourself and look for the dessert bar. After all, stressed spelled backward is desserts.

item.title: Dealing With Friend Grief
item.description:
Friends

Dealing With Friend Grief

What it is, why it's normal, and how to process this type of ambiguous loss.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Friend grief is common and natural as life happens.
  • Friend grief is a form of ambiguous loss and often difficult to process and make sense of.
  • It's common to minimize this experience or avoid it all together.
  • There are strategies to help you process this type of grief.

There has been a theme in my practice recently: friend grief. This entails grieving the loss of meaningful friendships and connection.

As we get older and life happens, we naturally change and evolve. We move away. We focus on or change our careers. We struggle with and prioritize our mental health. We navigate difficult life events and trauma. We partner up or get married. We have children or choose to be childfree. We take on new interests and move on from old ones. We have new priorities. We make changes to our lifestyles. We start to develop other friendships or connections. And with these life events and experiences come changes and shifts in our relationships.

Oftentimes, these changes in our friendships are not spoken out loud. But they are felt. Sometimes it's the physical distance that makes it hard to stay connected in the same way. Sometimes a friend slowly becomes less available. Sometimes you start having less and less in common with someone you used to have so much in common with. Sometimes you simply just don't like who this person has become and feel less inclined to maintain the relationship because of how it makes you feel.

Regardless of the circumstances, friend grief can be painful. Even if this friend is still in your life, but to a different degree, it's normal to mourn the relationship you once had and the closeness you previously experienced. Some of the things you might grieve or miss include the phone calls, the text chains, the inside jokes, the memes exchanged, the belly laughs, the experiences shared, and the support you offered one another.

Additionally, friend grief is often accompanied by other feelings, which can be overwhelming and/or confusing. You might also feel relief, abandonment, guilt, or shame—or some combination of these emotions. Again, this is normal and a common experience.

Friend Grief Triggers

Even if you have had some time and space, grief often persists. As grief expert David Kessler has said, "Where there is love, there is grief." And you will notice that it waxes and wanes and can be triggered by different things. Some common triggers include:

  • Seeing this friend post or be active on social media
  • Birthdays (yours or your friend's), certain anniversaries, and/or holidays
  • Moments of loneliness and disconnection
  • Spending time with new friends
  • Spending time with mutual friends
  • A big life event or accomplishment
  • The mention of their name
  • Seeing an old picture
  • Reflecting on past memories and stages of life

Processing Friend Grief

There are different reasons why people struggle with processing their friend grief. Sometimes it feels silly or insignificant compared to grieving the death of a loved one. And in these instances, it's common to minimize this type of grief. Other times, it may feel uncomfortable, or even intolerable, to confront this loss. This may result in avoidance and denial. Regardless of the reason, it's incredibly important to honor and make space for grief and any other feelings that arise from this loss.

Here are some strategies to help you process your friend grief:

  • Journaling: Journal your raw thoughts and feelings. It doesn't have to be flowery or poetic. Think of journaling as an exercise to externalize your inner experience rather than holding it all in.
  • Letter writing: Write an unsent letter to this friend. This letter can include all the things you have wanted to say, wish you had said, or the goodbye you never gave. You can then shred or burn this letter to symbolize letting go.
  • Engaging in therapy: If you have a therapist, make it a point to explore and process this grief in session. If you don't have a therapist, you may consider looking for one who specializes in grief, ambiguous loss, or life transitions. It can be helpful to confide in someone who will hold space and encourage the release of emotions.
  • Practicing self-compassion: Instead of dismissing these feelings of grief, try to name the feeling(s) and offer yourself love, patience, and understanding through kind words and language (i.e., "this is a significant loss," "it's okay to feel sad") or gentle touch (i.e., give yourself a butterfly hug, stroke your arm or shoulder, rest your head gently on your hands).

If you are wrestling with friend grief, know that you are not alone. This loss is significant, and it's important to be tender with yourself as you grieve.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Helping Patients Feel Safe Enough to Be Seen
item.description:
Trust

Helping Patients Feel Safe Enough to Be Seen

Small gestures create a safe space for open communication.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Patients often reveal their most critical information at the end of a consultation.
  • Attachment theory may help explain why patients can be reticent during medical appointments.
  • The steps a health provider can take to create an environment of trust are surprisingly ordinary.
Source: Olga Bereslavskaya / iStock

How many times in your life have you walked into the room of someone you barely know, stripped down to your underwear or less, and revealed intimate details about your life and personal habits, all within the space of 10 minutes?

This scenario highlights how much courage is required to attend a routine doctor’s appointment. We expect our patients to tell the truth and to reveal what’s going on underneath their symptoms.

They may have to talk about drinking, eating, sex, bowel movements, loneliness, fear, the medication they haven’t even opened, the symptoms they’ve Googled at three in the morning, or their worry that something is seriously wrong. Picture yourself doing all that while a virtual stranger takes notes, looks at their screen, and surreptitiously glances at the clock when they think you’re not looking.

We expect people to share so many intimate details when they barely know us, and I’ve lost count of how many times a patient has turned to me as they’re about to leave my consultation room, their hand hovering above the door handle. They might say, “There’s one more thing.” Or, “Could I ask another question?” Then the real consultation begins.

Behavior That Makes Patients Hesitate

Am I contributing to this delayed trust? And how can I help the people in my care feel safer sooner? I know how I act when I’m running late because my wife and family are excellent mirrors. I fidget in my chair and start looking at the door, mentally preparing my "to do before lunch" list. The professional version of me may still be listening, sprinting down the diagnostic tree, faithful to my training, while the personal me is already wondering how on earth I will get everything done and still show up for the kids’ concert.

Hubris might tell me I’m concealing this rather well, but I’m probably not. People notice when our hand moves to the keyboard too quickly or when we fill a silence that, if left untended, might otherwise have allowed something difficult to emerge. They are aware when we’re not with them and monitor us for evidence: Is it safe to trust? I've become much more curious about why we as humans are so sensitive to these signals.

The Role of Attachment Theory

Attachment theory gives us a lens that might sharpen our understanding. As children, we discover early what happens after we cry, get scared, make mistakes, or express our needs. If someone responds consistently, we may come to expect that it’s safe to show our distress or discomfort and that help will be there when we need it. When that response is less reliable, different ways of protecting ourselves may come to the fore. One of those lessons: When help doesn’t come, we had better fend for ourselves.

That might explain why a patient who has spent 50 years trying not to inconvenience anyone wouldn’t abandon that habit just because she has walked into my consulting room.

Simple Actions to Create Patient Trust

Amy Edmondson’s research on psychological safety shows the importance of speaking up without fear of humiliation or punishment. There is something useful here for medicine to explore, too.

Some of my patients remember surprisingly little of the specific information I’ve given them during a consultation, particularly if their condition is considered serious. What they do report back, often years later, is how they felt while they took it in. I like to think we have some control over that environment.

Here are three very ordinary actions that I have learned from my patients to create trust:

  1. Sit down.
  2. Leave the silence alone.
  3. Ask, “Is there anything else you’re worried about?” Wait for the answer.

None of these require new technology or another hour in the day.

The Old-Fashioned Business of Paying Attention

Medicine has changed enormously during my career and will no doubt continue to develop. Artificial intelligence is already becoming useful in diagnosis, while wearable devices can accurately track our health whether we’re snoozing or exercising. As a young doctor, the possibilities of precision medicine would have blown my mind. These days, I would add a note of caution: The increasing sophistication of our tools doesn’t make the old-fashioned business of paying attention obsolete.

The most useful thing I learn in a consultation rarely comes from a scan or blood test. It comes from waiting long enough for someone to say, "There's one more thing." I still don’t always get this right. I interrupt, and I get distracted. Undoubtedly, there is more than one patient who never got to say what they wanted to say to me. But I’ve become much more interested in that hovering hand. Now, whenever I hear “There’s one more thing,” I sit back down.

item.title: Jane Goodall and Donald Griffin Helped Us Get Over Ourselves
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Jane Goodall and Donald Griffin Helped Us Get Over Ourselves

These two leading researchers laid the groundwork for current animal research.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Goodall and Griffin challenged the idea of a sharp line between humans and other animals.
  • Both argued evolutionary continuity makes it unlikely that consciousness and sentience are uniquely human.
  • Evidence of animal sentience demands animal protection.

Over the past decade or so, there have been far fewer people wondering if nonhuman animals are in fact conscious, emotional, sentient beings. Ample comparative research clearly shows they are, and the important question at hand is why consciousness and sentience have evolved, not if they have evolved. Why are they crucial adaptations for being able to negotiate complex, challenging, and often ever-changing dynamic social and non-social worlds?

When one pays close attention to what we have learned and continue to learn about the nature of animal minds, it's very clear that it's anti-science data denial to claim that nonhumans aren't highly intelligent, conscious, sentient beings.1 Indeed, several countries have declared that nonhuman animals, including household companions and members of wild species, are sentient beings.

I was most fortunate to work very closely with Jane Goodall and had many wonderful conversations with Donald Griffin, the so-called "Father of Cognitive Ethology", two major contributors to the study of animal minds. Many people have asked me about their long-term contributions to the field, so it's my pleasure to offer a brief review to situate their outstanding, tireless work.2 in essence and for a wide variety of reasons, animals had lost their minds because of rampant data denial, and these two scientists among others helped them rightfully regain them.

Jane Goodall and Donald Griffin: Contrasting Styles, Similar Views

Jane Goodall arrived at Gombe Stream in Tanzania in 1960 with no undergraduate degree. She was sent there by Louis Leakey, and years later earned a PhD in ethology. Her main method of study was patience—slow watching. She was quite the acrobatic fieldworker, often climbing trees, and her team continues to study these fascinating beings 67 years later.

Source: Jane Goodall Institute/with permission.

Goodall's contribution to the study of animal minds didn't involve experiments. Rather, she and her colleagues recorded social strategies, long-term relationships, observational learning, and what resembled cultural variation in how groups used tools. Spurred on by Goodall, other researchers also observed that chimpanzees have various traditions that are passed on socially and are not simply inherited patterns of behavior. They also learned that mothers played a major role in shaping their offspring’s behavior and social status.

Goodall's views on the emotional lives of animals were more direct than Griffin's. Without hesitation, she noted that chimpanzees displayed a wide variety of emotions, including happiness, sadness, fear, and despair, and argued that their emotional lives are very similar to ours and that we had to seriously consider this fact when discussing them and us.

One of her most compelling early observations was the rapid change in the behavior of Flint, a young chimpanzee, after the death of his mother Flo. Flint stopped eating, withdrew from the group, and died within weeks. Goodall unhesitatingly described this as grief. She also documented strong mother-infant bonds, reconciliation and consolation after fights, and rituals such as rhythmic “waterfall dances” which she speculated might reflect something like wonder or awe.

Goodall also focused on individual differences among the chimpanzees. She gave her subjects names including David Greybeard, Flo, and Fifi, instead of numbers, which was considered unscientific at the time. She also freely spoke about their unique personalities and temperaments, two practices that were "forbidden" back then. But she insisted that this was perfectly okay and continued to do so for decades. Treating each animal as being highly unique became considered to be real "data" and changed how the public came to understand these and other animals. Her work had a major effect on mine.

Donald Griffin and Goodall sharply contrasted. Griffin conducted highly controlled experiments along with observational data for many different species, including bats, bees, birds, and nonhuman primates, and asked what they suggested about awareness. He focused on animal awareness and used behavioral flexibility as a marker of consciousness, and he took seriously the possibility of consciousness in insects and other invertebrates long before this was mainstream. Behavioral flexibility means an individual is evaluating their situation, considering past experiences, and deciding what to do based on the present moment and imagined future interactions. It is closely aligned with being sentient, which means being aware of and feeling what is happening to them and around them, and changing their behavior. We now know that a large body of scientific evidence stemming from studies of diverse species clearly shows that many animals are conscious sentient beings.

All in all, Griffin concluded that animals were capable of conscious thoughts and subjective experiences. Animal emotions were not a primary concern. On the other hand, Goodall's work on animal minds focused largely on their emotional lives, social relationships, and personalities rather than on more abstract arguments about consciousness.

In short, Griffin made it respectable to ask whether animals think and feel, and Goodall showed, through years of close watching, what a plausible answer might look like for one species.

Coda: Moving Beyond Human Exceptionalism

Both Goodall and Griffin challenged the idea of a sharp line between humans and other animals. Both argued that evolutionary continuity makes it unlikely that mind, emotion, or intelligence are uniquely human.

Griffin didn't write much on what "being conscious" meant about how animals are treated until around 1992, sixteen years after his highly controversial book The Question of Animal Awareness was published. I had some lengthy chats with him about this, and in the foreword to his seminal book Animal Minds: Beyond Cognition to Consciousness, he wrote about Dale Jamieson's and my work.

I was at the meeting where he first talked about The Question of Animal Awareness, his bold and unexpected book, and some people thought he had lost his mind! One comparative psychologist accused him of "muddled thinking" and suggested that cognitive ethologists should "hang up his field glasses, become a cognitive psychologist, and have nothing further to do with talk about consciousness or intention." Goodall’s concern was more explicit and became her public mission. She criticized invasive laboratory research on chimpanzees, advocated for habitat conservation, and founded the Jane Goodall Institute in 1977 and Jane Goodall's Roots & Shoots youth program in 1991.

The abundant scientific database that already exists—a body of evidence that has been available for a long time and just keeps growing—supports the fact that there exist many species of nonhumans who are undeniably sentient; deeply feeling, emotional beings who care about what happens to themselves and others. The fact of sentience needs to be put to use and into practice to protect and respect the lives of the other animals our species interacts with in so many ways.

We must stop pretending that we don’t know this-or-that about animal sentience. While we persist in pondering the obvious, ignoring what we already know and have long known, countless nonhuman victims continue to be abused by humankind, every minute of every day, planet-wide.

item.title: Reciprocal Mentorship: Why Intergenerational Arts Matter
item.description:
Social Life

Reciprocal Mentorship: Why Intergenerational Arts Matter

Age segregation has costs, but shared creative work can help heal communities.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Age segregation harms both young and old in society, with measurable mental health effects.
  • Reciprocal mentorship, where both groups teach and learn, creates genuine mutual benefit across generations.
  • Arts programs document measurable outcomes: increased belonging, purpose, and community connection.
  • Intergenerational engagement through creative outlets can address a root cause of loneliness across ages.

By Maya Lakshman, MPH

When I was in high school, I spent my afternoons in a retirement home across the street from campus visiting with a resident. What started as a weekly visit became two to three visits a week. We would watch old black-and-white films she loved when she was young, make art together, and she’d tell me about her life. High school is tumultuous and isolating. Being 80 in a retirement home, I learned, can be, too. Through spending time together, we each stepped outside the isolation of our separate worlds; as a result, we both felt less lonely. I didn’t understand the mechanics then, but what we both experienced—the quiet power of being needed, of having someone show up week after week, of creating something together—is exactly what community-based knowledge and a growing body of research now show: intergenerational connection works.

This scene repeats itself across the United States, though mostly unseen. In Montgomery County, Maryland, high school students and adult artists co-design creative workshops in affordable housing communities through Arts for the Aging’s Empower Project. In the American South, Alternate Roots—a 50-year coalition of artists and community organizers—brings together emerging and veteran creatives in social justice work (Merin, 1977). In Los Angeles, parents and children sit together making altars for Día de los Muertos, co-creating around cultural traditions through programs like Multigenerational Afterschool Arts (Kane & Kunisaki, 2025). These programs reflect the understanding that different ages need each other.

Our contemporary world segregates by age in ways that would astound people living just 150 years ago. Schools for the young. Workplaces for the “productive years.” Retirement facilities for the old. This age segregation is remarkably recent; a product of early-20th-century industrialization and its drive for efficiency (Freedman & Stamp, 2021). Graded education, child labor laws, Social Security, and mandatory retirement all contributed to the reshuffling. Sun City, which opened in Phoenix in 1960, pioneered the modern age-segregated retirement community. In contrast, 19th-century America was thoroughly age-integrated: multigenerational households, mixed workplaces, even almshouses that housed the old, young, orphaned, and poor together.

The cost of this segregation runs in both directions and is measurable. Young people may lose consistent relationships with adults who’ve navigated complexity and failure, and a sense of historical continuity that can anchor identity (Freedman & Stamp, 2021). Older adults lose something equally vital: the felt sense of being needed. Research shows that people over 60 who live in age-segregated communities experience higher levels of loneliness (Kim and Choi, 2025). A 2018 survey found that the two loneliest groups in America are younger people and older people—the very populations most separated by design (Freedman & Stamp, 2021). Social isolation and loneliness are linked to higher risks for depression, cognitive decline, heart disease, and early mortality (Hodgson et al., 2020; National Institute on Aging, 2019). Purpose, or the concrete experience of being relied upon, is an exceptionally strong predictor of mental health and longevity (Boyle et al., 2009; O’Súilleabháin et al., 2026). When that sense of purpose is ripped away, the same neurobiological threat response triggered by chronic loneliness is activated (Eisenberger and Cole, 2012).

For communities of color, age segregation compounds existing healthcare barriers. Traditional mental health services are often inaccessible due to systemic racism, historical harm, and documented mistrust in the medical system (Alang, 2019). Community-based arts spaces, rooted in cultural knowledge and embedded in neighborhoods, reach people that formal systems do not. Research shows that culturally tailored, community-led arts programs improve mental health outcomes in underserved communities and create what researchers call “essential social infrastructure” for mental wellness (Aguirre et al., 2025; Hand & Golden, 2019; GBHI, 2024).

The programs that work best operate on a principle increasingly recognized in intergenerational research: mutual benefit rather than hierarchical mentorship. Traditional models, such as younger people “helping” elders or elders “sharing wisdom,” recreate the hierarchies we’re trying to dismantle. Instead, effective programs support what researchers call “equal group status,” where both ages are genuinely needed to complete the work and knowledge flows bidirectionally (Cheng et al., 2026; Jarrott, 2023).

Arts for the Aging’s Empower Project pairs high school artist assistant fellows with adult artists in residence. Both are paid and are equal decision-makers. Young people and professionals learn from each other, and both contribute to designing and leading workshops for their community (Arts for the Aging, 2026). Alternate Roots works similarly. A younger artist reflected: “Older, more experienced people shared resources that helped my personal development. Later, I generated opportunities for others.” (Clark et al., n.d.). This is reciprocal mentorship.

The evidence for what this creates is substantial. The Wallace Foundation’s study of 35 community-based arts organizations across eight U.S. cities, which followed youth of color over 18 months, documented measurable outcomes: increased sense of belonging, skill mastery, sense of purpose, leadership development, and community connection (Osai et al., 2025). Such intergenerational programming can have positive rippling effects on mental health and well-being for both generations, and across the lifespan (Arring et al., 2026; Jenkins et al., 2021; Park, 2015).

Furthermore, studies show that arts-based programs reduce mental health stigma (Beato et al., 2024; Gaiha et al., 2021). More recent research examining intersectionality-informed art interventions with Black, Indigenous, and People of Color girls ages 14-16 found that art-based work supported narrative agency, processing of intergenerational trauma, and community connection (Birnkammer et al., 2026).

Why does this work? In part, it is due to biological factors. Chronic loneliness activates threat-response systems throughout the nervous system (Eisenberger and Cole, 2012). Being part of a genuine collaboration and feeling needed activates the reward system. Creative work engages the brain differently compared with talk therapy; it is embodied, non-verbal, and grounded in making something material. There’s also something that neuroscience alone may not be able to measure: these programs offer the felt experience of belonging across differences, of mattering to someone. They offer reciprocal vulnerability.

These programs also provide something foundational: spaces where genuine connection across ages is built, and where respect is reciprocal. Where in your community could genuinely reciprocal creative work happen, and what would it take to build such a space?

~~~

Maya Lakshman, MPH, is a doctoral candidate at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, where she uses neuroimaging, geospatial, and qualitative methods to understand the impacts of structural and interpersonal violence on development and mental health across the lifespan. She is a writer, educator, and researcher with an interest in translating evidence into equitable, justice-centered public health policy.

item.title: Gen Z, Careers, and Money: Navigating an Uncertain Future
item.description:
Career

Gen Z, Careers, and Money: Navigating an Uncertain Future

Making room for a meaningful life today while investing in your future.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Economic uncertainty is challenging traditional expectations about career success and financial security.
  • Spending on experiences can provide enjoyment and a sense of control when the future feels uncertain.
  • Small financial decisions can support or limit future flexibility, even when larger goals feel out of reach.
  • Aligning spending and saving with personal values can make room for both present and future you.

Co-written by Huong Diep and Jason Wang.

You've probably heard the advice: Work hard, build a career, and save for the future. But how much does that reflect the working world you're navigating?

The employment landscape keeps changing, with AI introducing new uncertainty about which jobs will exist, which skills will matter, and what building a career will require. Meanwhile, the income you are working toward may not seem sufficient to afford the life that work is supposed to make possible, making your future feel uncertain too.

Questioning what work can promise

You may have watched others devote years to an employer and still lose their jobs. Perhaps you have pursued an education, developed skills, and taken your career seriously, only to encounter limited opportunities or disappointing pay.

Dedication and hard work do not ensure an employer’s loyalty, and careful career decisions cannot always protect you from economic shifts.

It makes sense to reconsider how much of your identity and self-worth you want to tie to productivity, professional status, or earnings. Losing a job or struggling to earn enough can have significant practical and emotional consequences, but these experiences do not mean that you lack ability, have not tried hard enough, or are worth less as a person.

Why enjoying life now makes sense

If homeownership, a wedding, having kids, or other traditional milestones feel financially out of reach, making sacrifices for them can feel less worthwhile. How much enjoyment are you giving up for something you may never be able to afford? Some milestones may not appeal to you anyway.

A concert with friends or a long-anticipated trip offers something you can experience now, without sacrificing for a future that may not be attainable.

However, this reasoning can shift into financial fatalism: If the future is so uncertain, what is the point of saving or planning at all?

Notice the all-or-nothing thinking. Not being able to guarantee a particular future does not mean you have no influence over what happens next.

Small purchases in the context of big questions

Meet John*, whose story reflects experiences we encounter among young adults in our practices.

John followed the conventional roadmap to success: solid grades, a four-year degree in a field that promised job security, extracurriculars, internships, and networking. Yet, he finds himself struggling to enter the workforce.

After submitting hundreds of applications, John is exhausted and increasingly discouraged. When he does land an interview, it may be with an AI interviewer, followed by being “ghosted” afterward. Still living at home with his parents, he feels stuck in a cycle with no clear way forward. He begins to wonder, “Why did I even go to college?”

For John, buying a concert ticket or treating himself to an iced coffee offers more than momentary pleasure. Choosing to spend money, and deciding what to spend it on, provides a sense of autonomy and control amid so much uncertainty. Enjoying his coffee is an escape before the slog of yet another job application. Having fun at a concert with friends lets him live in the present, instead of always feeling weighed down by the pressures of building a life and career.

Let’s be clear: An occasional iced coffee now is not why homeownership might be out of reach later. At the same time, relatively small amounts saved and invested when you are young can grow by compounding over decades in ways that are difficult to fully appreciate today. Similarly, what will be within financial reach (and what you will want to purchase) in the future is hard to predict today. Debt can also build over time, as balances accumulate and interest or fees add to what you owe, creating significant financial strain.

As financial psychologists, we empathize with John's frustration while also recognizing an important tension: The very spending behaviors that help young adults cope with feelings of powerlessness in the short term may begin to create a pattern of spending (and even a sense of financial identity) that will not be helpful in the long term.

Money set aside might help you move, change careers, or leave an unhealthy workplace. Planning can help you prepare for needs and choices that differ from the milestones you originally imagined.

Of course, if your income barely covers necessities, saving may not be possible. That financial constraint should not be treated as a failure of discipline or willingness to plan.

What makes the present meaningful?

Spending on a nice dinner or vacation with friends can be enjoyable. But how much of its meaning comes from the setting, and how much comes from having time to connect?

If connection is important to you, there may be other less costly ways to experience it: cooking together, taking a regular walk, or simply making time to talk.

Investing time in friendships, family, and community can support both your present and your future. You can enjoy those relationships now while building connections that deepen and provide support through life’s changes.

Keeping the difficult questions open

There is no easy answer to how much you should invest in your career, save for later, or spend today. Your circumstances matter, and the balance may change over time.

What matters is continuing to grapple with important questions over time, and letting the answers evolve as your life evolves. Ask yourself:

  • How can I invest in my career when employer loyalty and job stability feel less assured?
  • How can I prepare financially for a distant future when traditional milestones feel unattainable or simply do not appeal to me?
  • What makes my life meaningful now, and are there ways to experience more of it that cost less?
  • What balance allows me to enjoy my life today while preserving choices for later?

Taking these questions seriously acknowledges what is outside of your control, while still helping you think about what you can shape, and leads to decisions that reflect your circumstances and values.

About the Guest Co-Author

Co-Author
Source: Dr. Jason Wang

Dr. Jason Wang is a licensed psychologist based in Washington, DC, specializing in the psychological dimensions of work, career, and money. His practice focuses on helping adults navigate life transitions and build more meaningful, sustainable, and values-aligned lives. Learn more at Inflection Points Therapy

item.title: When AI Saves a Fast Heartbeat, Who Carries the Conflict?
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

When AI Saves a Fast Heartbeat, Who Carries the Conflict?

AI writes the apology. Women often do the cleanup.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • AI can produce professional communication without necessarily producing understanding or accountability.
  • Navigating conflict can help develop judgment, boundaries, and relational competence.
  • Women may become responsible for resolving problems that polished communication leaves untouched.

You just hired an entry-level employee. A week later, they miss an important deadline, affecting several other projects like dominoes.

Your follow-up email carries an edge, and, within seconds, their reply hits your mailbox:

“Hello, I sincerely appreciate your feedback and understand the importance of timely delivery. I take full accountability and remain committed to improving our processes moving forward.

Best,

Employee”

For a moment, it may feel like a perfect reply. Their acknowledgment of your feedback and promise to do better feels almost like a relief, but at the same time raises a red flag: Why haven't they offered any explanation for what happened, and will their mess-up and apology be a repeat?

Conflicts, even minor ones, can raise our heart rate, especially at work, where professional reputation and job security may be at stake. We may act in a way that leads to regret later, and a reality check against AI may not be wrong. I call it "resolution illusion" when a message displays the signs of "this is what the opponent would most like to read in the reply", such as empathy, acknowledgment, and professionalism. At the same time, the underlying problem remains untouched, and that may even build some resentment. This may eventually lead to major conflict.

In an August 2026 Big Think interview, Terence Tao compared scientific research to hiking toward a waterfall. AI, he suggested, can work like a helicopter that takes you straight there. The hike teaches you the terrain, and a wrong turn might lead to a discovery you never set out to make. This, of course, isn't just about hiking.

In any situation, people seem to learn better through understanding and making mistakes. In conflicts, they have to decide what to say after what is already said and/or done. They may question their assumptions and build their own future behavioral "protocol" in similar instances, after considering how their actions may affect themselves and others.

In the workplace, in particular, they may need to revisit where instructions were unclear or ask for help they should have requested sooner; it is all part of getting lost, which leads to new professional discovery. That learning process may be uncomfortable, but it gives them practice in building their professional role, critical thinking, exercising judgment, speaking up, and establishing personal limits around work. When AI-polished responses are sent within a second, it becomes easier to skip the uncomfortable but necessary path for professional development, from A — the missed deadline — to B — figuring out what went wrong and what needs to change in this case.

In a 2025 survey, knowledge workers reported thinking less critically about tasks they were more confident AI could handle (Lee et al., 2025). In a separate experiment, readers perceived AI-assisted messages as less reflective of the sender’s own values than messages described as entirely human-written.

Philosophers Lai and Archer (2026) stated that relying on AI for emotional communication can deprive people of opportunities to discover what they truly value and who they really are. In the workplace, this is especially important, since it is where most people spend the majority of their time. An apology may sound like the product of reflection even if the sender skipped the necessary steps (remorse, responsibility, impact, and the desire to repair). This is only one part of the issue. The other is: If the reply makes the issue look settled, who absorbs the relational fallout?

Research on unrewarded work suggests an answer. In a study published in the American Economic Review, Babcock and colleagues examined tasks everyone wants done, but no one wants to do, such as writing a report or serving on a committee. Women were more likely than men to volunteer for these tasks, to be asked to do them, and to say yes when asked. The reason was not that women preferred this work. In mixed groups, people expected women to say yes, and in all-female or all-male groups, the difference disappeared (Babcock et al., 2017). Cleaning up — making sure everyone understood what went wrong and what not to do in the future — after a polished AI reply is this same kind of work that may fall to women.

A woman asked to fix what a polished reply left unresolved can use the following three questions to hand the thinking back to the person who made the mistake: What happened? What will you do differently in the future? How will you know it started working? The questions give the employee a simple checklist and a chance to reflect, explain their side of the story, propose a fix, and take responsibility for following through. For high-achieving women, the relevant boundary may no longer be knowing when to say no; it may be knowing when not to perform another person's unfinished thinking.

Imagine the employee had said what they were actually thinking:

"Hello, I thought someone said it's due Friday.

Best,

Employee"

Now the manager has something to work with – the scheduling issue, miscommunication, role clarification, and how the process works.

The manager learns how the employee understood the process, who they depend on, who depends on their work and responsibilities, and who to speak with. Exchanges like this can serve as a reference point in case of similar problems.

A polished message that solves conflict skips all that, allowing the same or more errors in the future, which may eventually lead to job loss.

It's not to say we shouldn't use AI for conflicts. Some workplace conflicts can be hostile, and for an entry-level employee, it can take time to spot; AI can help organize a timeline, clarify thoughts, brainstorm ideas, or find words for a boundary they already understand. This allows them to express themselves to the best of their knowledge and genuinely mean every word of an AI-assisted reply. The end product is what matters — the next deadlines should be handled based on the lessons learned from the first mistakes.

Conflicts may raise your heart rate, and AI can save a heartbeat, but it should not become another person’s unresolved conflict tomorrow.

item.title: The Turkey Trot Trap: Exercise Isn’t Currency
item.description:
Eating Disorders

The Turkey Trot Trap: Exercise Isn’t Currency

Why you don’t need to use exercise to “earn” your Thanksgiving dinner.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Using exercise as currency to “earn” holiday meals is compensatory exercise, which predicts disordered eating.
  • Joy and pleasure are basic human rights, not conditional rewards we must earn through productivity or labor.
  • Move on Thanksgiving only if it brings you joy; skip the run if you dread it, and enjoy dinner guilt-free.

Each Thanksgiving, nearly 1.3 million Americans participate in a Turkey Trot, typically a morning run with a cute name and sometimes a cute T-shirt. With over 1,500 events organized each year, Thanksgiving is officially the biggest race day of the year. And why do people wake up early on a holiday, when school and work are closed, to run in the cold?

AI will give you plenty of reasons: family bonding, charity, or just dodging kitchen duty. But the real reason most people lace up in the freezing cold? To “earn the feast.” It sounds like an innocent joke, but clinically, treating movement as currency to pre-pay for calories is known as compensatory exercise. When workouts become a tool to cancel out guilt, research shows, it stops being healthy movement and starts predicting disordered eating.

I want to push back on the idea that we need a psychological pass for a holiday meal.

When we turn joy into a transaction

Food is many things: fuel, culture, comfort, and community. And, holistically, culture, comfort, and community can all be pleasurable. Americans have a complex relationship with pleasure; we’re always vacillating over whether pleasure is a human right or a thing to be earned.

We all know, or maybe have been, the friend who cannot (insert something fun) until they’ve zeroed their inbox, cleaned the house, or crossed off the to-do list, and somehow we never quite balance the books. Whether we forgo the fun or dilute it with guilt, we never think we’ve done enough to earn our relaxation.

“Do I deserve this?”

This issue of feeling undeserving of pleasure comes up in so many therapy sessions. Trying to leave a bad relationship—do I deserve better? Wanting to pursue your passion—have I done enough to earn the right to follow my dream? Exhausted by a life of obligations—can I do something that is not in service of my job or my kids?

If we distill our culture into two teachers, one teacher tells us we need to earn our pleasure by working hard and being good. And since hard and good are never defined, we always feel like we haven’t yet earned the right to pursue pleasure. The other teacher tells us that life is short and to go find the joy. I’d argue that right now, that teacher is not the one hosting the Turkey Trots.

Thanksgiving. Friendsgiving. A holiday where we share one meal with loved ones we don’t see often enough. A holiday where we feel warm nostalgia as we eat the same pie we’ve had since we were kids. A holiday where we get to see elderly relatives, possibly for the last time. A holiday where we laugh in the kitchen, watch football, spend time with people we love, and yes, eat—because it’s a meal. Why do we think we need to earn any of this? We are allowed to pursue pleasure—in food, in friends—simply because we are human.

Trot for joy, not as a tax

And so, the Turkey Trot. My advice:

  • If the Turkey Trot brings you joy through being outdoors, moving your body, and being with friends or family, then trot away. Enjoy!
  • If the Turkey Trot brings you no joy, skip it! (Go help the person in the kitchen. Wash a dish; keep them company.) Research confirms that forcing yourself through exercise you dread doesn’t build sustainable health habits.
  • If you enjoy the Turkey Trot, but your brain tells you, “Phew, now you’ve earned tonight’s meal,” talk back to yourself. Remind yourself that you deserve joy, and that includes deserving Thanksgiving dinner.
  • And if you’re one of the thousand people who organize a Turkey Trot in your community, I beg you not to start the race by making a “joke” about your participants earning their Thanksgiving dinner. We all deserve pleasure, and if you stop acting like we need to earn it, maybe we can all start enjoying our lives a bit more.

item.title: How Thinking Outcomes Can Be More Important Than Being Right
item.description:
Decision-Making

How Thinking Outcomes Can Be More Important Than Being Right

Are mistakes made in caution really mistakes?

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Good decisions often prioritize consequences over the satisfaction of being right.
  • A low-cost precaution can be worthwhile even when the feared event is highly unlikely.
  • Open-mindedness and skepticism can coexist: preparing for a risk need not mean believing in it.

A few months back, I wrote a piece here about the viral conspiracy that Earth would lose gravity for 7 seconds on August 12th. I discussed how, despite not actually believing that the event would occur—because of a slew of reasons—the open-minded part of me (albeit still skeptical) nevertheless suggested developing a quick “just in case” protocol for the unlikely event. I received some positive feedback on how I exemplified the importance of cautious thinking throughout the piece and how, in context, we can engage two important dispositions towards thinking (Dwyer et al., 2016): open-mindedness and skepticism. On the other hand, though, some implied a level of foolishness in my thinking.

The latter cohort, I believe, missed my point, and so I aim to make it clearer in this follow-up. In that previous piece, I stated on multiple occasions that I didn’t actually believe the event would occur. In fact, I highlighted why it was nearly impossible.

But I used this event prediction as an example to make the point that cautious thinkers are typically happy to make minor mistakes in efforts to avoid risk, even if the risk is extremely low. That is, through cost-benefit analysis (consistent with many existing cost-benefit models we commonly see in psychology; e.g. Lave and March 1975; Thibaut and Kelley 1959; Uehara 1990), good thinkers may often choose a 99 percent likely mistake made out of caution, if the mistake yields minimal negative impact (e.g., looking foolish in front of one’s spouse). This will be selected over doing nothing potentially “foolish” (e.g., in light of being 99 percent “sure”), despite the disastrous impact that 1 percent chance would have because they failed to act (e.g., if the event occurred, death would be a near certainty if we were outdoors).

Simply, good thinkers don’t care about labels of wrong or right; they care about the outcomes of their decisions. It’s cautious thinking… and critical thinkers are cautious thinkers.

It’s much like hope for the best, plan for the worst. It’s why we develop contingency plans; it’s why we buy insurance. It’s largely why I don’t go outside in a thunderstorm, despite the odds against getting hit by lightning. It’s why I buy a lotto ticket once every few weeks, when the thought occurs to me on the day of a draw (i.e., I will not notice the loss of a couple of euros [thankfully], whereas winning the lotto would be life-changing). You never know.

With that, context (as well as moderation) is key. It might be foolish to buy too much insurance, to spend €200 weekly on the lotto, or to waste your time hiding in a cellar for three hours during your run-of-the-mill thunderstorm. Again, caution is considered in terms of cost (be it time, money, or status) relative to benefit or risk avoidance.

From an epistemological perspective, an established truth is that we cannot see into the future (as of yet, anyway [there’s some doozy of a meta-joke in there]). We do not know what’s going to happen. Objectively, we can place likelihoods on certain events happening, but that’s it. It’s our human interpretation that labels these probabilities as impossible, unlikely, possible, likely, highly probable, definite, etc. We might say definite, but that’s not exactly a guarantee. Consider the late Daniel Kahneman’s work on weather and stock forecasting (see also Kahneman, 2011). If we lived in a world of certainty (which we don’t), you’d never hear the phrase, “Well, that was unexpected.”

In moments of excitement and uncertainty, good thinkers are able to quickly evaluate probabilities, not just in terms of odds, but in terms of interpretation of outcomes (e.g., consider naturalistic decision-making [Klein, 2008]). The ability to do this quickly is a result of previous consideration and reflective judgment on priorities and values—things for which good thinkers would be concerned and cautious. They apply these considerations efficiently, if and when they need to. For example, despite less than a half-percent chance of your school burning down during your tenure in that school, how many fire drills were you a part of as a student? A lot, right? But you knew what to do in case it was for real.

Bizarrely, what’s your plan for a zombie apocalypse? Stop for a moment and think about it... Did your answer come to you fairly quickly? Even in the extreme unlikelihood of such a thing happening, it’s likely you thought about it or something similar before, at least once.

There’s nothing wrong with considering such things. Planning in such a way is a good cognitive exercise. It’s also good for creativity!

Cautious people often think in similar ways. Such cautious thinking might get accused of being “overthinking.” But that’s not necessarily a bad thing, unless it becomes a common or costly focus. Indeed, catastrophizing can be problematic. Moderation is important. But so too is caution, especially when it comes to ensuring good outcome-focused thinking. So, don’t sweat making small mistakes in life, especially if it’s done out of calculated caution. There’s nothing foolish about it.

item.title: How Music Can Help Us Move Through Climate Anxiety
item.description:
Climate Anxiety

How Music Can Help Us Move Through Climate Anxiety

Climate anxiety can paralyze us. Making music together can help us move again.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • We feel climate change through our interactions with water, heat, and air.
  • Climate anxiety tends to isolate us. Making and sharing art turns it into something we can carry together.
  • Culture is both a driver and an enabler of climate-health action.
Flow performing at the WHO Health Pavilion, COP31. Credit: EarthSonic / In Place of War.
Source: By Felipe Pagani

In November, at the WHO Health Pavilion at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, a packed room of climate scientists and policymakers got to their feet and danced. On stage, a collective of women musicians played songs built from the sounds of water: melting glaciers, swollen rivers, rising seas. After two weeks of talk about emissions, clean energy, and finance, the climate crisis stopped being something we discussed and became something we felt, together, in our bodies.

Many of us know the opposite feeling: another headline about record heat or flooding, a jolt of dread, and we scroll on, more alone with it than before. Climate anxiety is a reasonable response to a real threat, but carried alone, it paralyzes us. In that room, something moved.

Water carries the story

Most people do not experience climate change as a graph. It is intense heat, difficult breathing, and worries about water: too little, too much, or whether it’s safe to drink. Women often carry the heaviest load, as do indigenous peoples, long keepers of these waters.

This COP also put health on the agenda by opening with a health day. The numbers explain why: The Lancet Countdown links fossil fuels and climate change to an estimated 3.3 million deaths a year from air pollution and extreme heat alone. The toll on our minds is harder to count, but it is just as real. Heat disrupts sleep and attention, and the slow dread of what is coming shows up as anxiety and paralysis. A WHO Europe report released during the summit, Strengthening Mental Health in a Changing Climate, links floods and wildfires to anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress, and calls for mental health to be part of climate policy.

What helps? The WHO report looked at 20 interventions in 15 countries. Most aimed to build resilience and agency close to where people live. Agency is exactly what the arts can help people find. Art speaks human.

As a drama therapist and scientist, I am interested in how art can help us—projects using music, storytelling, and film to amplify the climate emergency. This isn’t therapy per se, but it draws on the same processes that creative arts therapists use with clients: giving form to hard-to-name feelings, and sharing them so they become bearable. It does two things that research and practice keep pointing to.

It invites people in as authors. Each artist found her own way into water. People engage differently when they are recognized as experts in their own lives.

It turns feeling into connection. In a survey of 10,000 young people in 10 countries, 59 percent were very or extremely worried about climate change. In my clinical work and in the classroom, I see people shut down when fear and grief have nowhere to go. Music gives those feelings a shared rhythm.

There is good reason to think this helps. Eco-anxiety is closely tied to difficulty regulating emotions, and a meta-analysis of controlled studies found that listening to music reduces anxiety. In a study that followed adults over three years, those who increasingly turned to music to manage their emotions also became more likely to tackle problems head-on. Music doesn’t only soothe. It can help us act.

"When we are emotionally and empathetically tied to the natural world, we are reminded at a more profound, instinctive level of our interdependence with it."—Yo-Yo Ma, in Music and Mind, edited by Renée Fleming

This echoes what my colleagues and I found in developing the WHO Europe-Jameel Arts & Health Lab policy brief on the role of the arts and culture in addressing the health impacts of climate change, and it reinforces findings from the first Culture Global Stocktake for Climate Action, also launched at COP31. Culture and cultural practices reflect and shape what we value, and it can build the trust and belonging that help people act on what they know.

An invitation

Listen to these sounds of nature. Then ask yourself: what is your relationship to water where you live? What would it take to protect it, together? Then let the listening lead somewhere. Review these six acts for water that help us move from feeling to understanding to action:

● Learn how much water your daily life uses.

● Adopt a few water-saving habits.

● Go deeper with films and talks from communities living with water crises.

● Join a group protecting rivers and oceans.

● Find out how you can help restore local wetlands, streams, and soils.

● Share your story. Make something with what comes up: a sketch, a few lines, a song. It doesn't have to be good.

If you work with young people or adults, try that last act as a group. Try a simple structure: open in a circle where people name what they feel; write a short song together from a local challenge, a mood, and a beat; perform it; then reflect on creating together rather than alone.

What I saw in Antalya gives me hope: a room full of committed people discovered they could still be moved, and could still move together. In my experience, hope is less a feeling we wait for than something we practice with others. The futures we can feel together are the ones we begin to build.
