item.title: 5 Steps to Prevent and Recover From Burnout
item.description:
Burnout

5 Steps to Prevent and Recover From Burnout

Regaining your biological heritage of adaptability to cope with rapid change.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • The accelerating speed of change and complexity are driving burnout.
  • Symptoms due to stress are signals of imbalance, not a badge of honor.
  • Recovery from burnout begins with self-acceptance.
  • Adaptability can be rebuilt through belief, recovery practices and a clear path.

Burnout is today’s number one concern.

It’s the number one question I get: “How can I cope with the feeling of overwhelm from all the stress and complexity in my life?” Sometimes the symptoms are physical or emotional. For others, the problem manifests in difficulty focusing, cognitive fog, and impaired performance. My experience validates the data indicating we are in a national crisis around burnout and the impact of how life is speeding up.

Stress and burnout are widespread. A 2023 APA survey, “Work in America,” revealed that 77% of workers reported experiencing work-related stress in the previous month (American Psychological Association, 2023). A similar Gallup poll reported that 27% of U.S. full-time employees felt burned out either very often or always (Gallup, 2026). There isn’t much consolation in knowing that you are not alone, other than that this indicates there are good reasons for your predicament.

Running on empty
Source: Stephen Sideroff/ AI generated illustration created by author using Microsoft Copilot

This trend that continues to accelerate is due to the gap between our ability to adapt and the exponential changes taking place in our society, along with how childhood survival learning freezes our ability to adapt. I’ve written about this previously: The 4 Horsemen of Stress: Why Managing Stress Is So Difficult | Psychology Today

It’s important to make sure that the symptoms you are experiencing are not held as a badge of honor or proof of how hard you work. They are signals of deep physiological dysregulation and that something needs to change. In this essay, I want to encourage you by presenting the first five steps you can take on The Path to recovery or prevention, and turning this into a challenge to reconnect with your biological ability to adapt. This is a route toward healing, recovery, greater resilience, and an adaptive biology better able to meet the world’s accelerating pace of change and complexity.

1. Acknowledge and Accept

Begin by honestly recognizing where you are, along with being willing to put energy into this process; such as with my resilience assessment to help you identify the patterns, pressures, and symptoms that need attention. It is important to acknowledge your starting point, so you accept that the road to greater resilience will take time and thus require your patience.

There is also a bigger role for acceptance in a world where so much is outside your control. This is a key to resilience. Everything you do requires energy. Yet, you have a limited amount of what I refer to as personal energy. Every time you hear about a tragedy in the media, or deal with a person who is unconsciously bothering you, it can easily trigger an emotional and physical stress response. Your mind-body goes into the stress fight-or-flight response, which drains your energy. But there is no benefit to this use of your energy, and at the same time, it takes away from your body’s ability to heal and recover. Solution: begin by recognizing that every stress you engage with drains your energy. Start making better choices about where you choose to send that energy. Decide to use your energy only where it can be of benefit.

2. Love and Accept Yourself

At the foundation of recovery is self-love: the belief that you deserve to be healthy and happy. Self-love includes accepting yourself – blemishes and all. My use of the word “accepting” doesn’t mean you like everything about yourself, but simply an acknowledgment of reality: This is where I’m at right now. The paradoxical theory of change states that growth begins with accepting where you are in this moment – because you can’t be anywhere else.

Judgments such as “I should be further along” or “I shouldn’t have made that mistake” ignore your reality and the truth in this moment. This carries the unconscious message that you are not good enough and is undermining. That interpretation often begins in childhood and can push you in the direction of burnout. Give yourself 30 days to follow this suggestion of radical self-acceptance. Then notice if it results in greater calm and peace, and perhaps a lessening of your symptoms. Note: the qualities of a healthy internal voice include loving yourself, being accepting and compassionate with yourself, as well as being supportive and caring. Treating yourself to this grounding will result in your fastest recovery and growth.

3. Honor the Path That Brought You to This Moment

You arrived here, in part, because you have been trying so hard. You want to do well; you put pressure on yourself and may have judged yourself too harshly. Recognizing that you are here not because you are defective, but because you have been striving so intensely, can make recovery easier. You are removing the stigma of inadequacy while owning your capacity. Take this challenge to be your best positive coach.

How can you translate your hard work and motivation to support your own self-care? Identify a practice of recovery, such as the use of meditation, a relaxation exercise, or biofeedback, that engages the parasympathetic branch of your nervous system. Think of this as a training that reengages your innate ability to adapt and recover.

4. Believe in your ability to adapt and break old patterns

We get stuck in old patterns. These patterns are a barrier to adaptation and growth. In fact, whenever you get close to breaking through to new ground, it can trigger uncomfortable or awkward feelings. (Tied to some form of “this isn’t me”.) These feelings then interrupt progress and cause you to pull back.

To break this pattern, I invite you to focus on your many accomplishments. You may already appreciate your successes, but it’s the identification of your skills and temperament that led to those achievements that translate results into belief in yourself. For success not to feel like it was magic, identify your unique ingredients that led to your successes. The hard work, the ability to set goals and focus, the persistence and the courage, and the skills that they demonstrate about you. These can be applied for success with new challenges. Use these to trust yourself to grow and establish a new pattern of balance and recovery, rather than burnout.

A key ingredient here is a willingness to sit with – to tolerate - the discomfort that comes from entering new territory. This is called, “growing pains”. A belief in your capacity to learn, recover, and respond differently based on a more accurate assessment of your achievements, creates the foundation for new habits and greater resilience. What you are simply doing is shifting your focus away from your shortcomings to your successes – and the skills and abilities you have already demonstrated.

This shift in focus will result in less fear or anxiety. And this is the foundation for regaining your ability to adapt. We have been conditioned to over-extend our stress response, while short-changing the opposite, the recovery response. Acknowledging your abilities creates the psychological space to take time to engage in the necessary recovery practices mentioned above.

Following The Path to Recovery
Source: Stephen Sideroff / AI generated illustration created by author with Microsoft Copilot

5. Define the path forward

One entryway to the healthy path forward is adopting a growth mindset. My previous steps led to this umbrella concept of how to engage with the world. It means that when you encounter something difficult and want to give up or distract yourself, instead, you remind yourself that this is a situation that is challenging you to grow and learn. I know that it’s easy to feel overwhelmed in this process. So many things to do and change and address. The key here is to have a map of the territory. This begins with knowing what The Path forward is. It is based on my 9 pillars of resilience. It’s a blueprint. Thus, whenever you take steps based on any of the 9 pillars, this puts you onto The Path. When you are on The Path you don’t have to worry about what you are not doing, as you are already achieving success for that day. (Focusing on what is, rather than on what isn’t.) This creates a powerful and practical framework that will consistently move you towards resilience, adaptation and away from burnout. In this article, I’ve already identified the first pillar – having a loving and accepting relationship with yourself; the fourth pillar – physical balance and mastery (engaging the recovery branch of your nervous system; the fifth pillar – mental balance and mastery – having a growth mindset; and the sixth pillar – emotional balance and mastery – tolerating the emotional discomfort of growth.

Bouncing forward

Resilience is about the ability to “bounce forward”. Not simply to return to your old baseline or pattern, but to use each stress to challenge yourself to learn, grow and move forward with greater awareness, flexibility and resilience.

Challenge yourself to follow these five manageable steps that put you on The Path and then appreciate the effort. And remember, successful recovery and adaptability will happen one step at a time.

item.title: How to Wash, and Boost, Your Brain
item.description:
Sleep

How to Wash, and Boost, Your Brain

Sleep better and increase your brainpower.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • The glymphatic system is very active at night cleaning your brain with cerebrospinal fluid.
  • When this process is disrupted with poor sleep, it contributes to neurodegenerative disease processes.
  • New evidence shows that even moderate amounts of alcohol impede the flow of cerebrospinal fluid.
  • There are ways to increase the flow of cerebrospinal fluid intentionally.
Wash your brain, support cerebrospinal flow, and improve your brain.
Source: Milad Facturian / Unsplash

What's at work while you are asleep

The glymphatic system contains glial cells, non-electrical cells in the lymphatic system that protect and cleanse. In 2012, a team of researchers (Maiken Nedergaard and others) proposed that this system primarily clears waste and is most active during deep sleep. (also called delta-wave sleep, a type of non-REM sleep). The glymphatic system is mostly made up of cerebrospinal fluid that clears waste such as amyloid-beta plaques and tau proteins. These waste particles are commonly found in clusters in the brains and other organs of people with neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington’s disease, as well as mood disorders (Zhang and colleagues, 2022).

Plaque clearance happens twice as fast at night when you sleep well. That's the good news. The bad news is that if your sleep is disturbed, waste is not cleared as efficiently. The natural ebb and flow of fluid is interrupted, and more waste particles accumulate.

Since this clearing occurs primarily in deep (delta-wave) sleep and not the other sleep stages, quality sleep is more important than quantity for the brain's night cleaning—more sleep does not mean better, and less sleep is not always harmful. The type of brain waves during sleep matters more than the eight hours you’ve heard about. The timing also matters. It is better to have deep (non-dreaming) sleep in several chunks toward the first half of the night. During a 90-minute sleep cycle, your brain dips into shallow sleep, then deep, then to shallow again.

What should I do to clean my brain, sleep better, and slow cognitive decline?

Stop alcohol use. Dr. Qinghua Liu and his team found that even moderate alcohol use reduces cerebrospinal fluid from entering and clearing plaques and proteins (Brain, Behavior, and Immunity, 2020). They also found that chronic moderate alcohol use led to increased activation of astrocytes—star-shaped cells that reactively try to address the extra inflammation from alcohol, thus reducing glymphatic function.

There is also a widespread loss of proteins that can polarize (shift across membranes) to move fluid and waste out. Over time, this loss is very difficult to reverse. Alcohol can clean a lot of things outside of our body, but it does not help cell function inside the brain or body. Stopping alcohol may be the single most important thing to begin cleaning your brain. Other depressant medications, like opioids, when used chronically, may also inhibit the flow and cleaning process of cerebrospinal fluid.

If my alcohol and opioid consumption is already at zero, what else can I do?

You may have already guessed that what helps keep cerebrospinal fluid moving and cleaning your brain also supports general health. However, knowing why can be helpful to keep you motivated. Here are four other things you can do and why:

  1. Move. Circulation through movement and cardiovascular exercise helps cerebrospinal fluid move. If you can't increase cardiovascular activity, try gentle movements of stretching or Qigong, no gym membership required. Rhythmic movements you can practice daily (without injury) are best.
  2. Focused attention and breathwork. A study by Keating and colleagues (2025) in Denmark found that focused attention, a type of mindful practice, directly increases cerebrospinal fluid flow (the opposite of what stress, aging, and neurodegeneration do to the brain). Focused attention can be brought to just about any activity. Sitting and breathing diaphragmatically also supports the rhythm and flow of cerebrospinal fluid (Yildiz and colleagues, 2022).
  3. Trust your brain and body. It’s hard not to experience fear about the repercussions of poor sleep, but worry compounds the problem. Instead, plan ahead. Use each night of poor sleep as an opportunity to slowly build a regular and rich mindfulness, breathing, or gentle movement practice that supports cerebrospinal fluid movement.
  4. Nourish and hydrate your brain. Like other diseases, eating well (good fats and lots of vegetables) and hydrating with healthy liquids (free of sugar, alcohol, and preservatives) also assists the rhythmic movement of cerebrospinal fluid. It’s hard to wash anything well without enough water; however, you may or may not need eight glasses per day. Whether you require more or less depends on your activity level, environment, and health status.

item.title: Failure Has Value in the Right Context
item.description:
Resilience

Failure Has Value in the Right Context

The hidden bias that prevents us from learning from our mistakes.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • When there is more chance of failing than succeeding, the lessons from success are more valuable.
  • Success reveals patterns that can be replicated, rather than one of many paths to failure.
  • Research shows that we try to avoid failure, or find it ego-threatening, which inhibits learning.
The odds favor success as a teacher.
Source: Christian Horz / Adobe Stock

Conventional wisdom says that we learn more from failure than success, and our culture tends to support this, often romanticizing failure as a noble precursor to accomplishment. Business literature encourages us to “fail forward” or “fail better”—phrases that have become as ubiquitous as they are clichéd.

I don’t agree with this.

We know that globally, around 70 to 80 percent of business start-ups fail within 10 years, varying by industry and region. But wherever you go, the chances of failure of a start-up are overwhelmingly greater than the probability of success. Take the example of 80 in 100 new businesses ultimately failing—that means there are 20 recipes for success and 80 for failure. If you succeed, you have discovered one of the 20 routes to success, whereas if you fail, you have experienced one of the 80 routes to failure.

In other words, in the case of a start-up business, experience of success is four times more valuable than experience of failure. Success will always be more instructive than failure when the probability of success is less than that of failure, which is virtually always the case in endeavors of impact and scale. They are never easy.

We are told that failure breeds resilience. Winston Churchill famously said, “Success is going from failure to failure without losing enthusiasm.” While that made sense in the bleak early days of World War II, when successes on the battlefield were rare, overall failure is overrated as a staging post on the path to success.

To be clear: I am not saying we can’t learn from failure, or that bouncing back from it isn’t hugely commendable and character-building. Importantly, the courage to fail emboldens people to try, and this is the bedrock of entrepreneurship and ultimately economic growth. But at an individual level, success is a better teacher.

At Discovery, we have learned from both success and failure, but our most profound lessons have come from learning what went right.

In 2008, we exited the U.S. health insurance market after eight years of trying to gain traction. Despite our efforts, we couldn’t attract enough members to create the scale to compete with incumbent giants. It was a very painful and instructive failure. And yes, we learned lessons that helped propel us onto the global stage. Today, instead of competing head-on, we partner with global insurers.

But what has been the biggest cause of our progress? Is it learning from our failure in the U.S.? Or is it the insights drawn from our success in incentivizing healthier behavior and turning that into a scalable global model known as Vitality?

Both have been important. But in my view, the lessons from success have been more transformative.

Why Failure Can Undermine Learning

The reasons why we learn more from success than failure lie in our psychology. Emotionally, failure is difficult to absorb. It feels bad. And when something feels bad, we tune out and don’t absorb the lessons as deeply.

Behavioral science shows that people tend to avoid personal bad news. For example, various studies show that up to 54 percent of individuals who undergo an HIV diagnostic test will not collect their results.

Cognitively, failure yields less useful information than success. Whereas success reveals patterns and principles that can be replicated, failure tends to be less instructional—it tells us what not to do but rarely illuminates what we should do.

Research by American motivational psychologists Lauren Eskreis-Winkler and Ayelet Fishbach, who aim to better understand the nature of success by studying failure, found that failure undermines learning. In their 2019 paper, “Not Learning from Failure—The Greatest Failure of All,” they reported on five studies with over 1,600 participants, who were asked a series of binary choice questions. For example: How much money do U.S. companies lose annually due to poor customer service? They were given only two possible answers to choose from: $60 billion or $90 billion. They were then given the correct answers to all questions and re-tested. Given that there were only two possible answers in each case, participants ought to have been able to remember the right one. But those who got the answer correct the first time did better on re-testing than those who got it wrong the first time. Why?

“Our society celebrates failure as a teachable moment,” they wrote. “Yet in five studies, failure did the opposite: it undermined learning. Why does failure undermine learning? Failure is ego-threatening, which causes people to tune out.”

In the field of medicine, a fascinating study from Harvard Business School—“Learning From My Success and From Others’ Failure”—tracked 71 cardiothoracic surgeons over 10 years and 6,500 operations. The research, by KC Diwas and colleagues, found that surgeons learned more from their own successes than from their own failures—and more from others’ mistakes than others’ successes. Why? Because others’ failures don’t trigger the same ego threat, so we tune in more readily.

Ironically, while failure demands resilience, it doesn’t always build it. Success does. It reminds us that winning and progress are possible.

Of course, there are times when failure is immensely instructive. Plane crashes happen so rarely that when they do, they present rich opportunities for learning. If you are flying a space shuttle, you are only as strong as your weakest link, and studying these allows you to avoid the same catastrophic outcome twice.

But in complex networked systems, where processes are not linear, and where the chances of failure are greater than the chances of success, it is success that teaches best.
